newsitem.title: GERMANY: Supreme court upholds complex German voting law.
newsitem.headline: Supreme court upholds complex German voting law.

text.p: Germany's supreme court on Thursday upheld the complex voting laws that assured Chancellor Helmut Kohl a working government majority in 1994 and helped ex-communists win seats in the Bonn parliament.

The court said loopholes that gave Kohl a 10-seat majority and let the ex-communists scrape in under the normal five percent minimum vote did not discriminate against any party and thus did not violate the constitution.

The decision means Germany's current election laws, which saved Kohl's majority three years ago by increasing it from two to 10 seats, will not be changed for the 1998 election when Kohl faces a tough fight for a record fifth term.

It also gave a boost to the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), the reformed successors to East Germany's hardline communist rulers who have divided the left-wing vote in the east and blocked any united opposition front against Kohl.
Kohl's Christian democrats (CDU) welcomed the decision and said with approval: "The current distribution of seats in parliament remains."
PDS parliamentary leader Gregor Gysi also hailed the ruling, adding: "The attempt to push the PDS out of parliament through a constitutional appeal has failed."
The eight judges were evenly split over the extra seats issue, showing how divided views were over the loopholes, but a split vote on the court amounts to a rejection.
The judges were unanimous in supporting the loophole that lets a party enter parliament with less than five percent of the vote if they win at least three constituencies outright.
Lower Saxony state, governed by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), brought the appeal to the supreme court.
Kohl's current majority would not have been endangered if the court had found the law unconstitutional, but such a ruling would have had hard-to-foresee effects for the next vote.
Bonn had to add 16 extra seats to its 656-member lower house of parliament in 1994 because of the so-called "overhang mandates" that resulted after the votes were counted.

Twelve of those seats went to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and four to the SPD. This assured him a 10-seat majority although his coalition was only barely ahead with 48.4 percent of the vote compared to 48.1 percent for the opposition.
These "overhang mandates" arise because of Germany's two-vote system, where each voter can cast one ballot for a specific candidate in one of the 328 constituencies and a second for a party.

The second vote is usually the more important, because it gives the percentage each party wins. But if a party wins more direct seats on the first ballot than it should have according to the second vote, new seats have to be created.

In old West Germany, there were never more than a few extra seats in each parliamentary session. But unification in 1990 changed voting patterns and produced a bumper crop of "overhang mandates" in 1994 and raised questions about the law.
Most of the extra seats were won in eastern Germany, where voters are less familiar with the complex law than westerners.
The second loophole, one almost never used in old West Germany, also concerns directly elected deputies.

Small parties are usually barred from parliament if they win less than five percent in their second ballot. But they can take up their seats if their candidates win outright in at least three constitutencies on the first ballot.
The PDS won 4.4 percent of the national vote in 1994 -- normally not enough to return to parliament -- but it also won outright victories in four east Berlin districts.
That gave it the right to take 4.4 percent of the seats in parliament and it ended up with 30 deputies.
This angered some conservative western deputies, who complained the ex-communists were using a loophole to get into parliament.
